title: Winn v. Brady
description: Whether a recorded judgment lien constitutes a constitutionally protected property interest, entitling junior lienholders to personal notice of an execution sale, and whether this rule should apply retroactively or prospectively.
plaintiff_argument: Junior judgment lienholders hold a constitutionally protected property interest and are entitled to personal notice of an execution sale, not merely notice by publication, to satisfy due process.
defendant_argument: The execution sale was not a state action, thus due process rights were not implicated, and they complied with statutory notice requirements by publication.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed that junior judgment lienholders are entitled to personal notice consistent with due process, but reversed the Intermediate Court of Appeals' decision to apply this rule to the instant case, holding that the new rule shall apply prospectively only.

title: Hawaii v. Zuffante
description: Whether the Hawaiʻi Constitution's due process clause requires law enforcement to record all in-station custodial interrogations and, when feasible, all outside-the-station custodial interrogations.
plaintiff_argument: The State of Hawaiʻi argued that recording custodial interrogations is not a due process requirement, relying on previous precedent that declined to mandate such a practice.
defendant_argument: Charles Zuffante argued that the failure to record his interrogation undermined his rights against self-incrimination, confrontation, and a fair trial, urging the court to adopt a recording requirement.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the Intermediate Court of Appeals' judgment and the Circuit Court's judgment of conviction and sentence, remanding the case for further proceedings consistent with its opinion that recording custodial interrogations is constitutionally required.

title: Grube v. Trader; State v. Rogan
description: Whether the circuit court erred in sealing judicial records without sufficient justification and in requiring a reporter to retain counsel to assert his constitutional right of access to those records.
plaintiff_argument: Grube argued that the circuit court failed to meet the procedural and substantive requirements for sealing records, that vague assertions of ongoing investigations were insufficient, and that he had a personal constitutional right to represent himself pro se in seeking access.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the circuit court properly identified a compelling interest in preserving the integrity of ongoing investigations, that the sealing order was narrowly tailored, and that Grube, appearing to represent a business entity, was rightly required to retain counsel.
decision_outcome: The court granted Grube's petition for a writ of mandamus, ordering the circuit court to unseal the documents and permitting Grube to represent himself in further proceedings, while denying the writ of prohibition as unnecessary.

title: Hilo Bay Marina v. State of Hawaii
description: Whether a state-imposed deed restriction requiring a landowner to use land for "church purposes only" violates the separation of church and state under the Hawaiʻi Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the deed restriction requiring land use for "church purposes only" constitutes state action that advances religion, violating the strict separation of church and state mandated by the Hawaiʻi Constitution.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the Hawaiʻi Constitution's Establishment Clause should be interpreted co-extensively with the U.S. First Amendment, and recent federal jurisprudence allows for government accommodation of religion, making the deed restriction permissible.
decision_outcome: The court ruled in favor of Hilo Bay Marina, LLC and Keaukaha Ministry LLC, overturning the Circuit Court's summary judgment for the State and granting summary judgment to Hilo Bay.

title: Foresman v. Foresman
description: Whether HRS § 657-1.8(a) violates the ex post facto clause of the United States Constitution by imposing civil liability for acts committed in 1975 and 1976 based on subsequently enacted criminal statutes, and whether the Circuit Court's erroneous jury instructions were harmless.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that HRS § 657-1.8 is constitutional and that any alleged error in jury instructions (using current statutes) was harmless because the defendant's admitted conduct would have been criminal under statutes existing at the time of the alleged acts.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that HRS § 657-1.8(a) violates the ex post facto clause by imposing civil liability for past acts based on subsequently enacted criminal statutes, and that the jury should have been instructed on criminal statutes in effect when the alleged acts occurred.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the ICA's Judgment on Appeal, which affirmed the Circuit Court's Final Judgment, despite finding that the Circuit Court erred in its jury instructions.

title: State v. Hoffman
description: Whether a defendant's un-Mirandized statements, made in response to police words or conduct "normally attendant to arrest and custody," are admissible if those words or conduct were reasonably likely to elicit an incriminating response, thus constituting "interrogation" under the Hawaiʻi State Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that Hoffman's statements were made in response to Officer Tavares’s statements or actions “normally attendant to arrest and custody” and therefore did not constitute “interrogation,” making them admissible.
defendant_argument: Hoffman argued that the ICA gravely erred by ruling that an officer's conduct and statements "normally attendant to arrest and custody" could not arise to an interrogation triggering Miranda warnings, meaning his statements should be suppressed.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the ICA's judgment and the circuit court's order, holding that some of Hoffman's un-Mirandized statements were made in response to interrogation and should be suppressed, while others, specifically his "okay, I'm done" statement during the scuffle, were not and should be admissible.

title: Surface Water Use Permit Applications
description: Whether the Commission on Water Resource Management's decisions regarding instream flow standards and surface water use permits for Nā Wai 'Ehā complied with constitutional and statutory mandates, protected Native Hawaiian rights, and avoided unlawful delegation of authority.
plaintiff_argument: The appellants (MMK, Hui/MTF, OHA, Mahi Pono, WWC) argued that the Commission failed to restore stream flows, did not justify its IIFS decisions, unlawfully delegated public trust duties, and violated due process rights in water allocations.
defendant_argument: The Commission contended that it properly set the IIFS, made reasonable water allocations, did not violate due process rights, and did not unlawfully delegate its authority.
decision_outcome: The court vacated and remanded the Commission's decision regarding the Interim Instream Flow Standards (IIFS) and the unlawful delegation of public trust duties, but affirmed the Commission's decisions on MMK's water allocation, Mahi Pono's due process rights, WWC's due process rights, and the Public Utilities Commission's jurisdiction.

title: State v. Tran
description: Whether Hawai'i's statute on continuous sexual assault of a minor and its related constitutional provision violate the U.S. Constitution's Sixth and Fourteenth Amendments regarding jury unanimity on specific predicate acts and the sufficiency of the indictment.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the circuit court erred in dismissing the indictment, that the Motta/Wells liberal construction standard should apply, and that the state's constitutional and statutory provisions do not violate the U.S. Constitution's Sixth and Fourteenth Amendments regarding jury unanimity on specific predicate acts.
defendant_argument: Tran argued that the state's constitutional and statutory provisions are unconstitutional under Ramos v. Louisiana because they permit non-unanimous jury verdicts on specific acts, and that the indictment was insufficiently specific under Jardine, thus violating his Sixth and Fourteenth Amendment rights, and should have been dismissed with prejudice.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the circuit court's order granting in part and denying in part Tran's motion to dismiss, affirmed the circuit court's denial of Tran's supplemented new trial motion, and remanded the case for further proceedings.

title: Kanahele v. State
description: Whether Act 14 of 1995 precludes claims regarding the 2018 designation of the Mauna Kea Access Road (MKAR) as a state highway, and whether the State breached its constitutional and fiduciary duties to Native Hawaiians by this designation.
plaintiff_argument: Plaintiffs argue Act 14 of 1995 does not bar their claims because the 2018 designation of MKAR as a state highway was a new breach of trust, occurring after Act 14's cutoff date, and constituted an illegal taking of trust lands without proper procedure.
defendant_argument: Defendants argue Act 14 of 1995 fully resolved all claims related to the Hawaiian home lands, including the MKAR, and that the 2018 designation did not create new claims, thus barring the plaintiffs' suit due to sovereign immunity and Act 14.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court vacated the circuit court's summary judgment in favor of the Defendants and remanded with instructions to grant summary judgment to the Plaintiffs, ruling that Act 14 of 1995 does not preclude the Plaintiffs' claims and that the State breached its trust duties.

title: Davis v. Bissen
description: Whether constitutional due process required a contested case hearing before the County of Maui could remove houseless plaintiffs and their belongings from County property.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that they possessed a constitutionally protected property interest in their chattels and that due process required a contested case hearing before the County could seize and destroy their property.
defendant_argument: The County argued that the plaintiffs did not have a constitutionally protected property interest in storing their chattels on public land, or that if they did, alternative procedures provided sufficient due process without a contested case hearing.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the circuit court's denial of the County's motion to dismiss as to plaintiffs Davis and Lau, holding that constitutional due process required a pre-deprivation contested case hearing for their seized personal property.

title: State v. Wilson
description: Whether the Hawaiʻi Constitution and the Second Amendment to the United States Constitution establish an individual right to carry firearms in public for self-defense, thereby invalidating Hawaiʻi Revised Statutes (HRS) § 134-25(a) and § 134-27(a).
plaintiff_argument: The State argues that HRS § 134-25(a) and § 134-27(a) are constitutional, that there is no state constitutional right to carry a firearm in public, and that these laws do not violate Wilson's federal constitutional rights.
defendant_argument: Wilson argues that HRS § 134-25(a) and § 134-27(a) violate his constitutional right to protect himself in public by carrying a lethal weapon, as conferred by both the Hawaiʻi Constitution and the Second Amendment.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the circuit court's order dismissing the charges against Christopher L. Wilson, ruling that Hawaiʻi's laws restricting the public carry of firearms and ammunition do not violate his constitutional rights.

title: State v. Lafoga
description: Whether the circuit court's decision to empanel an anonymous jury, without strong justification and without taking precautions to mitigate prejudice, violated the defendants' constitutional rights to a fair trial, presumption of innocence, impartial jury, and effective assistance of counsel.
plaintiff_argument: The State implicitly argued that the anonymous jury was permissible or that any error in empaneling it was harmless, and that the court took reasonable precautions.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the anonymous jury violated their constitutional rights to presumption of innocence, an impartial jury, effective assistance of counsel, and an impartial tribunal, constituting structural error requiring a new trial.
decision_outcome: The court upheld the circuit court's decision to empanel an anonymous jury, concluding that any error was harmless.

title: State v. Hewitt
description: Whether Cyrina L. Hewitt was in custody for Miranda purposes while being questioned by police in a hospital bed, thereby requiring Miranda warnings before her statements could be used as evidence.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that Hewitt was not in custody at the time of questioning, and therefore, Miranda warnings were not required.
defendant_argument: Hewitt argued that she was subjected to custodial interrogation without the requisite Miranda warnings because she was in custody, even before probable cause developed, due to her medical condition and the circumstances of the police questioning.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Hawaii reversed the Intermediate Court of Appeals' judgment that ordered a remand and affirmed the district court's judgment of nolle prosequi for both counts against Hewitt, effectively dismissing her convictions.

title: Ohana v. Univiversity of Hawai'i
description: Whether the burden of proof shifts to the government in constitutional challenges to administrative rules based on Article XII, Section 7 of the Hawai'i Constitution, and what standard governs such challenges.
plaintiff_argument: The Flores-Case 'Ohana (FCO) argued that the burden of proof should shift to the government and that the Ka Pa'akai framework, which requires agencies to consider the impact on Native Hawaiian rights, should apply to administrative rulemaking.
defendant_argument: The University of Hawai'i (UH) promulgated the rules. The Attorney General (amicus curiae) argued that the burden of proof should remain with the challenging party and that the Ka Pa'akai framework, designed for contested cases, should not apply in the same way to administrative rulemaking because rulemaking does not produce an evidentiary record.
decision_outcome: The court held that the burden of proof remains with the challenging party, but affirmed that the Ka Pa'akai framework applies to administrative rulemaking, requiring agencies to conduct a contemporaneous analysis of Native Hawaiian traditional and customary rights before adopting rules. The case was remanded for further proceedings.

title: State v. Canosa
description: Whether a sixteen-month delay in sentencing deprived the defendant of due process and a fundamentally fair sentencing proceeding, and whether this delay rendered the defendant's allocution constitutionally inadequate.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the delay did not prevent the court from legally resentencing the defendant, nor did it constitute a waiver of the State's right, and that the defendant's claims were waived.
defendant_argument: Canosa argued that the sixteen-month delay in sentencing violated his due process rights and right to allocution, especially because the ordinary maximum terms of imprisonment had expired before resentencing, making the extended sentences illegal.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the Intermediate Court of Appeals' judgment, ruling that the State's unreasonable delay in sentencing deprived the defendant of due process and a fundamentally fair sentencing proceeding, and ordered his immediate release with a sentence of time served.

title: State v. Obrero
description: Whether Hawaiʻi Revised Statutes (HRS) § 801-1, which requires a grand jury indictment for felony prosecutions, was implicitly repealed or superseded by a 1982 constitutional amendment allowing felony charges via preliminary hearing.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the 1982 constitutional amendment to Article I, Section 10, effectively nullified HRS § 801-1's grand jury protections by authorizing the State to use complaints and preliminary hearings to initiate felony prosecutions, and that HRS § 801-1 was implicitly repealed.
defendant_argument: Obrero argued that HRS § 801-1 plainly requires a grand jury indictment for felony prosecutions not within district court jurisdiction or chargeable by information, that the statute has not been implicitly repealed, and that the State's use of a preliminary hearing after a grand jury no-bill is unconstitutional.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the circuit court's denial of Obrero's motion to dismiss, ruling that the State cannot subject Obrero to trial and sentencing without a grand jury indictment as required by HRS § 801-1.

title: State v. Sagapolutele-Silva
description: Whether the existence of probable cause alone is sufficient to establish that a suspect is in custody for Miranda warnings, or if a totality of the circumstances test must always be applied.
plaintiff_argument: The State argues that the totality of the circumstances test should be used to determine custody for Miranda purposes, and that probable cause is relevant but not dispositive.
defendant_argument: Sagapolutele-Silva argues that while probable cause is not determinative, she was in custody under the totality of circumstances during the traffic stop and OVUII investigation, requiring Miranda warnings.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the district court's order suppressing Sagapolutele-Silva's statements and the ICA's judgment affirming custody during the traffic stop, clarifying that the totality-of-the-circumstances approach applies and Sagapolutele-Silva was not in custody until after the SFST.

title: Hicks v. 2021 Hawaii Reapportionment Commission
description: Whether the 2021 Hawaiʻi Reapportionment Plan is valid, specifically regarding its adherence to constitutional and statutory guidelines requiring representative districts to be wholly included within senatorial districts where practicable.
plaintiff_argument: The petitioners argued that the 2021 Hawaiʻi Reapportionment Plan is invalid because it failed to give adequate effect to the constitutional and statutory guidelines requiring representative districts to be wholly included within senatorial districts where practicable, and that the Commission abused its discretion.
defendant_argument: The Commission argued that it satisfied its obligations by considering the constitutional and statutory district within district guidelines, which are discretionary, and that the petitioners failed to demonstrate an abuse of discretion in adopting the Plan.
decision_outcome: The court denied the petition, ruling that the 2021 Hawaiʻi Reapportionment Plan complies with article IV, section 6 of the Hawaiʻi Constitution and HRS § 25-2(b).

title: League of Women Voters of Honolulu  v. State
description: Whether a bill that undergoes a non-germane amendment must restart the constitutional three readings process in each legislative house.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that Act 84 was unconstitutional because the bill's substance was entirely changed by a non-germane amendment, requiring new readings in the Senate, which did not occur.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the Legislature's rules permit a bill to be read by title only and do not require new readings after amendments, even if the content is entirely substituted.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the circuit court's summary judgment for the State and remanded the case with instructions to grant the plaintiffs' motion for summary judgment, ruling Act 84 invalid.

title: In re Individuals in Custody of the State
description: Whether the Supreme Court of Hawaii should grant extraordinary relief to order the expedited release of certain inmates and mandate specific public health measures in correctional facilities during the COVID-19 pandemic, or if existing legal mechanisms and changed circumstances render such relief unnecessary.
plaintiff_argument: The Office of the Public Defender (OPD) argued that the COVID-19 pandemic created an unprecedented public health emergency requiring extraordinary relief, including the expedited release of certain categories of inmates and court-ordered public health measures in correctional facilities, to protect inmates and the public.
defendant_argument: The respondents (DPS, prosecuting attorneys) argued that conditions had changed since prior petitions, with widespread vaccine availability and a federal settlement addressing pandemic response in correctional facilities, making the requested extraordinary relief unwarranted and that existing legal mechanisms for inmate release were sufficient.
decision_outcome: The court granted the petition in part, ordering the Department of Public Safety (DPS) to comply with HRS § 353-6.2 regarding periodic reviews and transmission of findings for pretrial detainees, but denied all other requests for extraordinary relief.

title: State v. Lee
description: Whether evidence obtained after police entered Joshua Lee's bedroom without a warrant should be suppressed, with Lee arguing it should be suppressed due to an unlawful search and the State arguing it should not be suppressed due to an emergency aid exception or because Lee's subsequent actions were new crimes.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the evidence should not be suppressed because an emergency aid exception applied, or alternatively, Lee's actions constituted a new crime, and the evidence was not "fruit of the poisonous tree."
defendant_argument: Lee argued that the ICA erred in vacating the suppression order, contending that the State failed to establish exigent circumstances to justify the warrantless search, which was inconsistent with the Hawai'i Constitution's enhanced protections.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the ICA's judgment, which vacated the circuit court's order to suppress evidence, but on different grounds, meaning the evidence will not be suppressed.
